title: Lab 6: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text: This lab examines whether people with higher Extraversion scores are more likely to endorse the Big Five item “Know how to comfort others” (A3). I expected a positive association because more outgoing people may have more opportunities to respond to others’ distress, which could be associated with greater confidence in knowing how to comfort someone. Because the item has ordered response categories, I used a cumulative logit model to estimate how the distribution of responses varies with Extraversion.

#Part 4. Fit and Interpret Cumulative Logit Models ## 4.1 Fit the Threshold-Only and Extraversion Models The A3 response categories have a natural order, and the distances between adjacent categories may differ. A cumulative logit model uses the order of the responses to estimate the probability of responding at or below each cutpoint.

stopifnot(all(a3_counts$n > 0))
m0 <- clm(A3 ~ 1, data = lab_data, link = "logit")
m1 <- clm(A3 ~ extra_c, data = lab_data, link = "logit")

4.2 Interpret the Thresholds at Average Extraversion

th <- m1$alpha
b <- coef(m1)[["extra_c"]]
cum_avg <- plogis(th)
cat_avg <- diff(c(0, cum_avg, 1))
endorse_avg <- 1 - cum_avg[3]

tibble(
  Response = response_levels,
  Threshold = c(unname(th), NA_real_),
  `P(Y ≤ j)` = c(unname(cum_avg), 1),
  `P(Y = j)` = cat_avg
) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = Threshold, decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(`P(Y ≤ j)`, `P(Y = j)`), decimals = 1) |>

#Part 5. Compare the Models and Interpret the Slope ## 5.1 Likelihood-Ratio Test

lrt <- anova(m0, m1)
lrt

title: Lab 6: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
section: 5.3 Interpret the Extraversion Slope on the Latent Scale
text:
5.3 Interpret the Extraversion Slope on the Latent Scale

middle_width <- mean(diff(th)[2:3])
fraction_of_middle_category <- abs(b) / middle_width

A one-point increase in Extraversion was associated with an upward shift of 0.84 units on the latent response scale. This shift was about 84.6% of the average width of the two middle response categories on that scale.

po_test <- nominal_test(m1)
po_test

Tests of nominal effects

        Df  logLik    AIC     LRT Pr(>Chi)
<none>     -3814.5 7641.0                 
extra_c  4 -3814.1 7648.2 0.83519   0.9337

po_df  <- po_test["extra_c", "Df"]
po_p   <- po_test["extra_c", "Pr(>Chi)"]

Allowing the Extraversion slope to vary across cutpoints did not significantly improve fit, χ²(4) = 0.84, p = .934. I retained the proportional-odds model.

title: Lab 6: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
7.1 Shared Cumulative Odds Ratio

or_tab <- tidy(m1, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "extra_c", coef.type == "location")

odds_change <- abs(or_tab$estimate - 1)
odds_direction <- if (or_tab$estimate >= 1) "higher" else "lower"

Each one-point increase in Extraversion was associated with 130.7% higher odds of responding above any given cutpoint, OR = 2.31, 95% CI [2.15, 2.48], p < .001.

section: 7.3 Predicted Probabilities for All Response Categories
text:
7.3 Predicted Probabilities for All Response Categories

pred <- ggpredict(m1, terms = "extra_c [all]") |>
  as.data.frame()

category <- as.character(pred$response.level)
category_index <- match(category, as.character(seq_along(response_levels)))

pred <- pred |>
  mutate(
    Extraversion = x + extra_mean,
    Response = factor(
      coalesce(response_levels[category_index], category),
      levels = response_levels
    )
  )

stopifnot(!anyNA(pred$Response), !anyNA(pred$predicted))

ggplot(pred, aes(Extraversion, predicted, fill = Response, group = Response)) +
  geom_area(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(drop = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
  labs(
    x = "Extraversion (subscale mean)",
    y = "Predicted probability",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







Figure 1: Predicted response probabilities for the comfort item from the proportional-odds model.





As Extraversion increased, the predicted response distribution shifted toward higher categories, with Very accurate becoming more likely.

title: Lab 6: Ordinal Logistic Regression with the Big Five
text:
7.4 Shared and Threshold-Specific Odds Ratios

bind_rows(
  tibble(
    Threshold = "Shared (proportional odds)",
    OR = or_tab$estimate,
    low = or_tab$conf.low,
    high = or_tab$conf.high,
    Model = "Shared"
  ),
  threshold_or
) |>
  mutate(Threshold = fct_rev(fct_inorder(Threshold))) |>
  ggplot(aes(OR, Threshold, colour = Model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio for responding above the threshold",
       y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")







Figure 2: Shared and threshold-specific cumulative odds ratios for Extraversion.





The threshold-specific odds ratios clustered around the shared estimate, and all confidence intervals lay above one. This pattern was consistent with the likelihood-ratio test and supported retaining a common slope across cutpoints.
